source.title: Beyond SAEs: Consistent Concept Discovery with Sparse Coding
source.authors: Jin-Ho Choi; Hyesu Lim; Jaegul Choo; Steffen Schneider

record.tranche_reason: The study compares features across dictionary sizes using decoder similarity and activation overlap, testing the splitting pattern with its own matching analyses rather than reproducing a single original SAE method.
record.gate_note: Rows cover cross-size feature correspondence and the reported semantic examples. General cross-seed consistency, reconstruction, utilization, and sparse-probing results are not rows because they do not measure splitting itself.
record.test_reason: Section 6.1 and Appendix E.2 (Figs. 6, 12, 15) compare 4× and 16× dictionaries within ConSDL, ReLU SAE and TopK SAE. They count consistent 4× atoms with at least two 16× counterparts at decoder cosine ≥0.7 and show example parent/child families. This is a different method (decoder-cosine matching with a cross-seed filter) aimed at the splitting-with-size question, so T2. The paper's headline topic is cross-seed consistency, and the splitting analysis is secondary.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but the record misplaces the emphasis. The paper's main conclusion is that ConSDL (per-sample sparse coding with refitting and co-active similarity regularization) gives more consistent dictionaries and coefficients across seeds than six SAE baselines. As secondary analyses, the authors conclude that larger ConSDL dictionaries capture multiple distinct but related finer features of broad concepts, while ReLU and TopK largely keep the broad atom. They do not claim results at billion-parameter scale.
record.recipe_differences: ConSDL uses per-sample FISTA sparse coding, coefficient refitting, and co-active similarity regularization; the study compares its scaling behavior with several SAE families rather than reproducing a single original SAE splitting setup.
record.method_sensitivity: The one-to-many pattern varies by SAE method: it is more frequent for ConSDL than for ReLU and TopK in the reported size comparisons. Tested dictionary expansions are 4× and 16×.

fits_no_version.finding: At the same dictionary width, consistent ReLU (and TopK) atoms more often have multiple ConSDL counterparts than the reverse, across four backbones. The Fig. 5 beer-bottle and Fig. 11 baseball examples show the same pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Different sparse dictionary-learning procedures at a fixed size decompose the same activations at different granularities, with one method's atom matching several of another's.

record.problems: The cross-size feature analyses rely partly on selected qualitative examples and cosine-based matching; union coverage of parent inputs is not measured. Experiments use four relatively small backbones, and the authors state that results at billion-parameter scale are not established.
record.rows_left_out: Left out results on general cross-seed consistency, dictionary utilization, reconstruction, sparse probing, and cluster agreement because they do not directly measure feature splitting or its predicted parent-child input coverage. They appear in Sections 5–6 and Tables 2–3, 6, and 8–18.

untested.parts: Whether the child features together cover the parent's inputs. The union of child activations is not measured.
All of it. Only 86M–162M backbones with SAEs the authors trained themselves; no large models and no open SAE releases. The authors say billion-parameter scale is not established.
Nesting across more than two sizes, and whether families mirror a concept hierarchy in the model's own representation.
All of it: no parent-child firing or absorption analysis.
All of it: no test that larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller ones, or of novel latents at each size.
Whether splitting says little about the model's own units. No cross-size splitting comparison for Matryoshka or other objectives beyond ReLU and TopK.

missing.what: In Pythia-160M, ReLU keeps a highly similar plant atom across 4× and 16× (cosine 0.95). This is a second contrast example with no row.
The ConSDL advantage in cross-size splitting is larger in vision and persists when ≥3 or ≥5 counterparts are required. Counts in both directions (4×→16× and 16×→4×) are in Fig. 15 but not recorded.

record.verdict_notes: ConSDL is not an SAE, so only the ReLU and TopK rows bear on V1 in the strict SAE sense; there splitting is present but weak. V2 is treated as untested: the backbones are 12-layer models of 86M–162M parameters, beyond a one-layer transformer but neither large models nor open releases. The record's limits_scope labels for V2 and V3 rested on untested parts and are removed. The example figures are hand-picked, and concept labels were assigned by an LLM.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not quantify whether the union of child-feature inputs covers roughly all inputs of the coarse feature.
Tests four named backbones, but not large models or open SAE releases.
It reports related feature families and some geometric and activation similarities, but does not establish a nested concept hierarchy or test whether it mirrors a hierarchy in the model.
No parent-child takeover or absorption analysis.
No test that larger latents decompose into combinations of smaller latents, or that every dictionary size adds novel latents and precludes a complete atomic set.
No causal test that the SAE objective produces splitting on correlated or hierarchical inputs, or that Matryoshka SAEs reduce it as an objective effect.

rows.subject: CLIP ViT-B/16
rows.size_stated: approximately 86M parameters; dictionaries at 4× and 16× expansion
rows.operation_detail: Compared matched ConSDL atoms across dictionary widths.
rows.measure: Number of larger-dictionary counterparts, decoder cosine similarity, pairwise similarity, and image-level activation overlap.
rows.baseline: 4× ConSDL atom associated with Golden Retriever
rows.value: One 4× atom corresponded to six 16× atoms with decoder cosine similarity 0.65–0.75; the 16× atoms had pairwise decoder similarity ∼0.5 and image-level Jaccard overlap 0.32–0.50.
rows.note: The authors describe the 16× atoms as capturing distinct attributes, including fur, tails, muzzle shapes, and puppies. The reported overlaps are partial; the union of child activations is not quantified.
rows.check: For V1 this is a full one-to-six split of a selected example: children have cosine 0.65–0.75 to the parent. Coverage of parent inputs is not measured, which is an untested part, not a weakness of the effect. ConSDL is per-sample sparse dictionary learning, not an SAE. The 86M-parameter backbone is not a large model, so drop V2. For V3 it is partial: the family is geometrically close, but no hierarchy is tested.

rows.subject: Pythia-160M
rows.operation_detail: Compared matched ConSDL atoms across dictionary widths.
rows.measure: Number of larger-dictionary counterparts, decoder similarity, and token-level activation overlap.
rows.value: One 4× atom matched four 16× atoms associated with plant species, crops, and flowers; 16× atoms had limited token-level activation overlap (0.11–0.21).
rows.note: The paper says the 16× atoms have low pairwise decoder similarity, but does not report a numeric cosine range for this example or quantify union coverage of the 4× atom's inputs.
rows.check: Selected example: a 4× plant atom matches four 16× atoms. No parent-child cosine range is given. Drop V2 (162M model, not an open release). For V3 it is partial, as in r1.
